I pasted this link in case anyone's interested in code I wrote for my personal workaround for some of the the issues solved by this PR, plus a few more.

It has a `DateOnly` object, named as a `DateStamp`, for example, and a `MonthStamp` object as well. (Those objects are not used in any hotpaths, so instead of writing them from first principles, I wrapped `DateTime` objects with them, but then provided an interface that represents the intention of the objects.) It also has a `TimeOfWeek` object that represents ideas like "10am on Monday".

The main emphasis of this library has a couple of features that are not addressed by this PR: 

1. Comparison of times in multiple timezones is extremely efficient due to resolving all times back to a utc-based `TimeStamp` object. It's like converting everything in your code to `DateTimeKind.Utc` but without the ambiguity and without giving user code the opportunity to accidentally put or deserialize a `DateTimeKind.Local` time where `DateTimeKind.Utc` was expected.
2.  Conversion of timezones is a lot faster than the conversion utilities provided by `TimeZoneInfo`. See the `TimeZoneCalculator` class. Conversion iterators for sequential timestamps is even faster by magnitudes.

Whilst `DateOnly` and `TimeOnly` ideas do solve some problems and are very much needed in the framework, an object that is unquestionably UTC time and quickly/easily converted between timezones is also needed (at least, by me). The library linked above provides this. For example, the `TimeStamp` object can add an absolute amount of time, or you can pass in a `TimeZoneInfo` object to the method and it will add the given amount of time accounting for timezone offset changes in the given timezone. 

Thanks for reading!

It's important with time-of-day operations, because *comparison* can only be done within a single day.   In other words, it is easy to test if "now" is between 1:00 and 3:00, but a lot more challenging to test if "now" is between 23:00 and 01:00, and even more challenging to have a single operation that can do both.

In pseudocode, given a `test` value, and the half-open interval `[start, end)` where all three values are a time-of-day on a 24 hour clock:

```
if start <= end
    isbetween = start <= test AND end > test
else
    isbetween = start <= test OR end > test
```

You can see how I implemented it in the corefxlab prototype here:

https://github.com/dotnet/corefxlab/blob/3c54492b3c4a8effee31b0700a4979feba9a3394/src/System.Time/System/Time.cs#L492-L507

This would definitely be useful. Sometimes I run into weirdness where I go adding a TimeSpan to a DateTime and get unexpected results because I think the DateTime's time part has been set to midnight (so it can be a "pure" date), but it actually hasn't. Having an explicit Date type would solve these problems; such a type would not be possible to "pollute" with time of day data.

On the usefulness/motivation front, this question was asked 10 years ago. 

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/5314309/a-type-for-date-only-in-c-sharp-why-is-there-no-date-type

There are lots of good comments in there, and a detailed reply from yours truly in 2016.  In particular, I appreciate this comment very much:

> A date only data type is to DateTime as an integer data type is to a decimal. Those who argue we do not need a date because you can just throw away the time part is akin to saying we do not need integers as we can throw away the decimal part. Our world has a concept of a date that does not include a time. 5 March is not 5 March 00:00:00.

> Best names for these types would be Date and Time but there is issue that VB already using these names and if we go with such names can conflict with VB.

Not to derail with bikeshedding the names 🙂 but I think it would be okay, possibly with a compiler update. There are already such conflicts with `String` and `Enum`; you can opt for the CLR type by bracketing the name, e.g. `[String]`, `[Enum]`

There's no conflict with `Time` as a class name, but there is precedence for calling it `TimeOfDay` - we have uses of this name already:

- [`System.DateTime.TimeOfDay`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.datetime.timeofday) and [`System.DateTimeOffset.TimeOfDay`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.datetimeoffset.timeofday) properties, both return `TimeSpan` that represent the time part of the date/time value.
- [`TimeZoneInfo.TransitionTime.TimeOfDay`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.timezoneinfo.transitiontime.timeofday) property, which is a `DateTime` whos date portion is ignored and time portion represents the time of day of the transition.
- [`Microsoft.VisualBasic.DateAndTime.TimeOfDay`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.visualbasic.dateandtime.timeofday) property, which returns a `DateTime` representng the current date and time of day, truncated to the nearest second.   (should be obsoleted, IMHO)
- [`Microsoft.OData.Edm.TimeOfDay`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.odata.edm.timeofday) struct and  [`Microsoft.Graph.TimeOfDay`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.graph.timeofday) class,  which are objects similar to the one we're proposing here, but with less functionality.

I couldn't find any interesting cases of just `Time`  Part of the problem with "time" is that it has multiple meanings.  The question is whether we want to use a name that has precedence for the intended meaning (`TimeOfDay`), or if we want to pick a name that reduces conflicts with existing code (`Time`) even if we have to rely on the meaning conveyed via xmlcomments/docs.

For `Date`, the main conflict is with the [`Date`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/visual-basic/language-reference/data-types/date-data-type) data type, which is a language reserved keyword, aliased to `System.DateTime`.  Sure, we could have a `System.Date` and VB.Net developers would either spell out `System.Date` or would use `[Date]`, but that might not be obvious in how it differs from the `Date` keyword.

Also it's worth noting that VB.Net has a date literal syntax - regardless of what names we pick, we should consider if such syntax should also be supported for either of the new types.  Example:

```vb
Dim d As [Date] = #8/13/2002#
Dim t as TimeOfDay = #12:14 PM#
```

There are a lot of  other places that use `Date`.  The interesting ones being:

- [`System.DateTime.Date`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.datetime.date) and [`System.DateTimeOffset.Date`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.datetimeoffset.timeofday) properties, both return a `DateTime` with time truncated, that represent the date part of the date/time value.
- [`System.Net.HttpWebRequest.Date`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.httpwebrequest.date) property, which returns a `DateTime` representing the value of the HTTP `Date` header.
- [`Microsoft.OData.Edm.Date`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.odata.edm.date) struct and  [`Microsoft.Graph.Date`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.graph.date) class,  which are objects similar to the one we're proposing here, but with less functionality.

There are some random projects that have `DateOnly` properties such as [`Microsoft.Office.Server.ActivityFeed.DateOnly`](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.office.server.activityfeed.activitytemplatevariable.dateonly) - but I don't think there's much risk there.

In summary, I'm most concerned with name conflicts of *objects* (in OData and Graph) and with the `Date` keyword in VB, but the other proposed names have precedence as well.  If we have strategies for dealing with such conflicts, then either choice of name is reasonable, IMHO.

Since I was tagged, here's a few additional thoughts after reading the comments thus far:

- Naming is important. The succinctness and meaning of the type should carry the most weight IMHO. I understand the consideration of other languages, but only VB has been called out up to this point. The `Date` keyword in VB is arguably _wrong_, but is a legacy carried forward from VB6 to make the migration to VB.NET easier. I would urge the consideration of the _most appropriate_ type name and let the VB team decide how it should be handled at the language level. I can think of several ways they _might_ handle it:
  - Add a new `DateOnly` keyword. That's closest to the suggestion, but is language-specific
  - Add a `Option DateOnly On` directive to toggle the primitive `Date` type to switch between meaning `System.DateTime` and `System.Date`
    - This has the additional benefit of being configurable at the \*.vbproj level for all files
    - Mixing both types is easy and natural since `Imports System` is already defined, for example:
      - `Dim d as Date ' with option, maps to System.Date`
      - `Dim dt as DateTime ' already possible today and easily understood side-by-side`
- Min/Max date is dependent upon a calendar. IMO it was a mistake on System.DateTime and we shouldn't repeat it. There are real scenarios in history and science applications where the date can go back further than `01/01/0000` (e.g. BCE) and higher than `12/31/9999`. The min and max values should be queried from a calendar instead.
- In a similar fashion, time is dependent upon a clock. This proposal assumes a 24-hour clock, which can also be easily divided and represented as a 12-hour clock. There are historical examples of older systems of time that are not based on a 24-hour clock. This could limit its use in some scientific applications. You can image this could also be a problem in spaces such as astronomy. Mars, for example, doesn't use a 24-hour clock; it's 25 hours.
  - This point is not to push for a _pie in the sky_ design, but rather acknowledge that a clock is to `Time` or `TimeOfDay` as `Calendar` is to `Date`. I think it's plenty reasonable to only ship a 24-hour clock out-of-the-box, but there must be some hook or abstraction for others to build upon
   - This also lends credence to removing `Meridiem` because it is dependent upon a specific clock (a 12-hour clock)
- I won't dispute that losing information is bad, but I feel this particular scenario is just a little different. We think of these two components as `Date + Time`. We don't think of `1.5` as `1 + 0.5`. Furthermore, the behavior is logically ambiguous when converting a floating-point numeric to an integer. What should happen? Truncate? Round? Choosing a behavior is implementation-specific and not clear to a user/developer. That definitely should not be allowed. However, I would argue that this is not true of date and time. In such an implicit conversion, the developer has already defined that they only want one of the two components. Outside the realm of `DateTime.Date` and `DateTime.TimeOfDay` we can observe many historical cases of getting just the date using `Now - TimeOfDay(Now)` and time using `Now - Today`. We tend not to see numeric conversions or rounding starting with `1.5 - (1.5 - 1.0)`. This will probably be a lost argument, but I imagine in practice that explicit casting will be prolific and unnecessary verbose.
- Addressing the name comflicts with existing properties can be solved with methods or extension methods. `DateTime.ToDate` and `DateTime.FromDate` would not only solve the conflict with `DateTime.Date`, but would be congruent with the established alternate conventions when implicit/explicit operator conversions are defined.

I don't think the comment on DateTime is correct. DateTime is always work with Gregorian Calendar and not any arbitrary calendar. Also, the original design of DateTime to support the year ranges 1..9999. This doesn't mean there is no years outside this range, but it means the DateTime design it intended to support only that range. This because we wanted to pack the whole struct in one long value (64-bit value). If type work on specific range, it makes a lot of sense to have Min and Max values.

@tarekgh I know original design of `DateTime`, but to say or limit it's design to the Gregorian Calendar is like saying the default string/character range should be ASCII instead of Unicode. Locale defaults are fine, but the universe doesn't resolve around a singularity. I'm well aware of the storage design, but that's an implementation detail. Optimize - sure, but don't let it completely dictate the design. I find it highly unintuitive that `DateTime` cannot represent any date or time. `DateTime` will **not** work with a Gregorian Calendar date in the future past 9,999 (e.g. it doesn't _always_ work).

I also disagree with your assertion:
>_"...this type is not going to work with any of these calendars."_

How can that be? A date is meaningless without a calendar. Today's date would simply be _"The 18th day of the 3rd month in the year 2021"_. To make sense that it's _"March 18, 2021"_ requires a calendar. I'm not suggesting that the `Date` type store any reference to a calendar, but you cannot make sense without it. In the same, not every number can be represented in intrinsic numeral types. There are several solutions, most notably `BigInteger`. If the intent is to limit the proposed `Date` and `Time` types to the constitute bounds of the `DateTime` components (so be it), then perhaps there should be a similar `BigDate`, `BigTime`, `BigDateTime`, and/or `BigDateTimeOffset`.
